title: Transverse and longitudinal waves
cards: Disturbance and travel are different

Waves transfer energy without an overall transfer of the medium’s material. A floating marker moves up/down as ripples pass rather than travelling across the whole tank. Air molecules vibrate around local positions as a sound disturbance travels.
Compare the oscillation direction

In a transverse wave, oscillation is perpendicular to energy-transfer direction. Water ripples are treated as a transverse example in this course, although real surface-particle motion is more complex. In a longitudinal wave, oscillations are parallel to travel, creating compressions and rarefactions. Sound in air is longitudinal.
Watch one marker

Follow the highlighted marker, not just the moving crest/compression. Its local repeated motion differs from the pattern’s progress. A slinky can demonstrate both directions, with care not to confuse the physical coil shape with the representation of air particles.
Predict the oscillation

Choose transverse/longitudinal and the travel direction. Predict whether oscillation is perpendicular or parallel. The dots show local oscillation while the disturbance crosses the view; they do not drift along with each crest. Shapes/amplitudes are exaggerated and not molecular paths.

title: Amplitude, wavelength, frequency and speed
cards: Name four wave quantities

Amplitude is maximum displacement from equilibrium, not peak-to-trough height. Wavelength λ is distance between adjacent equivalent-phase points, such as crest to crest or compression to compression. Frequency f is cycles per second in hertz. Period T is time per cycle: T=1/f.
Use v = fλ
Wave speed is frequency times wavelength. For f=5 Hz and λ=0.4 m, v=2 m/s. All waves obey the wave equation. Use metres for wavelength and seconds for time. Rearranging gives λ=v/f and f=v/λ.
Changing medium

Frequency is fixed by the source. When a sound wave enters a medium with a different speed, wavelength changes in proportion to speed at unchanged frequency. This explicit speed/frequency/wavelength transmission requirement is separate Physics. It does not mean amplitude or energy transmission must stay unchanged.
Make a wave prediction

Choose frequency and wavelength; predict wave speed. Markers oscillate locally and crests move across a ruler. The horizontal distance represents model wavelength while playback is slowed; visual speed is illustrative and the numerical ledger supplies SI values.

title: Measuring waves in water, solids and air
cards: Choose suitable apparatus

Required practical8 (separate) or20 (Trilogy) investigates frequency, wavelength and speed in a ripple tank and in a solid. Use a vibrating source, shallow water, illumination and a scale for ripples; use a vibrating string/cord with a signal generator for waves in a solid. Keep electrical equipment appropriately separated from water and control volume/amplitude.
Measure repeated intervals

Measure several wavelengths then divide by the number of complete wavelength intervals to reduce relative reading error. Determine frequency from source calibration or count cycles over a timed interval. A strobe/frozen image can help read a pattern, but avoid confusing it with an actual stationary wave or a different strobe alias. Calculate v=fλ.
Measure speed of sound

Use two microphones a measured distance apart with a data logger/oscilloscope to measure arrival delay of a pulse; v=distance/time. An echo method needs twice the reflector distance for the out-and-back path. Avoid hand timing a short sound journey; long baselines and repeats improve resolution. Record methods, uncertainties and controls.
Analyse a ripple measurement

Choose measured length covering four wavelengths and source frequency. Predict speed using λ=length/4, then v=fλ. Generated images/data are ideal; they prepare for judging apparatus suitability and real measurements rather than establish hands-on competence.

title: Reflection, transmission and absorption
cards: Three outcomes at a boundary

A wave arriving at a boundary can be reflected, transmitted or absorbed. Absorption transfers energy into the material. Reflection changes travel direction back into the original medium; transmission carries energy onward. The proportions depend on materials, wave and surface conditions.
Measure from the normal

Draw a normal perpendicular to the surface where the ray meets it. Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, both measured between ray and normal. A ray diagram represents travel direction, not the oscillation direction. Mark arrows on both rays.
Prepare the light practical

Separate required practical9 investigates reflection by different surfaces and refraction by different substances. Use a ray box, narrow slit, surface/block, paper and protractor. Trace rays, mark the boundary and normal, measure angles from the normal, repeat and compare surfaces. Avoid looking into a bright beam and use school procedures.
Predict the reflected ray

Choose incidence angle and smooth/rough surface. Predict the local reflection angle for an individual surface facet. Roughness changes the facet normals and scatters a beam even though each local reflection obeys the law. The model uses a representative labelled facet, not a roughness distribution.

title: Sound, solids and hearing
cards: Sound crosses different materials

Sound can travel through solids as vibrations. A vibrating solid can set nearby air into pressure oscillations; air sound can make a solid vibrate. These conversions happen in loudspeaker cones, microphones and the ear. They are mechanical waves and need a material medium.
From air to the ear

Pressure oscillations vibrate the eardrum and other structures in the ear, producing the sensation of sound through further biological processes. The conversion works over a limited frequency range. A schematic eardrum is not a complete anatomical or hearing-diagnostic model.
A limited hearing range

Normal human hearing is approximately20 Hz to20000 Hz (20 kHz). Individual sensitivity varies and can change with age or damage. Frequency influences pitch; amplitude/intensity influences loudness. Ultrasound is above the upper human hearing limit, not necessarily louder sound.
Classify a frequency

Choose frequency and the supplied normal hearing range. Predict whether it falls within the range. The animation shows an exaggerated air compression driving a solid membrane; its playback rate is unrelated to the actual audible frequency.

title: Ultrasound, sonar and seismic evidence
cards: Echoes reveal hidden boundaries

Ultrasound partly reflects at boundaries between media. Measure the return time and use supplied wave speed: one-way depth=vt/2. Different speeds, absorption and reflection can reveal structures inside objects. Medical imaging and industrial flaw detection exploit these differences.
Sound the sea

High-frequency echo sounding sends a pulse toward an object/seabed and records a reflected signal. The pulse travels out and back, so divide total path length by two. A single speed is an approximation if the medium varies. Multiple echoes can indicate several boundaries.
Seismic waves probe Earth

Earthquakes generate longitudinal P-waves that travel through solids and liquids at different speeds, and transverse S-waves that cannot travel through liquid. Arrival times, paths and shadow regions provide evidence for Earth’s internal structure and core. The model is evidence-based inference, not direct viewing of the core.
Predict an echo depth

Choose supplied wave speed and round-trip time; predict one-way distance. Watch a pulse travel out and back. The scale and playback are exaggerated. The single-boundary homogeneous-medium model omits scattering, variable speeds and signal processing.

title: The electromagnetic spectrum
cards: One continuous family

Electromagnetic waves are transverse and transfer energy from a source to an absorber. All types travel at the same speed in vacuum, about3×10⁸ m/s; the GCSE specification also treats their speed in air as the same. They do not require a material medium.
Order the bands

From long wavelength/low frequency to short wavelength/high frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible (red to violet), ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma. These named groups form a continuous spectrum rather than seven isolated wave speeds. Human eyes detect only the visible band.
Frequency versus wavelength

At fixed speed v=fλ, higher frequency means shorter wavelength. A radio and gamma wave in vacuum have very different wavelengths but equal speeds. Their interactions with matter and potential uses differ; visible colours occupy only a narrow portion.

Choose frequency in MHz and a multiplier. Predict vacuum wavelength using λ=300/f when f is in MHz. The animated wave is a schematic transverse trace, not a literal electric-field magnitude or an audible oscillation.

title: Refraction at a boundary
cards: Draw the boundary and normal

Refraction is a change of wave direction at a boundary when the speed changes and incidence is oblique. Draw a normal at the incidence point, mark travel arrows and measure both angles from it. A normal-incidence ray changes speed without bending.
Toward or away from normal

On entering a slower medium, an oblique ray bends toward the normal. On entering a faster medium, it bends away. Frequency remains set by the source, so changing speed changes wavelength. The drawn medium is an ideal transparent region, not a material identification test.
Measure with a block

Trace incident/emergent rays through a transparent block, mark the block outline, remove it and draw the internal path. Compare several angles, keeping ray width small and reading the protractor from the normal. This prepares the refraction part of separate practical9; common students still construct refraction ray diagrams.
Predict the bend

Choose faster/slower destination and normal/oblique incidence. Predict toward, away or no bend. Exact illustrative angles are supplied rather than using a required Snell-law calculation. The model omits dispersion, partial reflection and total internal reflection.

extra.title: Higher: wavefronts explain the turn
extra.text: When one part of an oblique wavefront enters a slower medium first, that part advances less while the other side still travels faster. The wavefront turns; its perpendicular ray turns toward the normal. Wavelength is shorter at the same frequency. Absorption, transmission and reflection can vary with wavelength and material.

title: EM production, absorption and radiation risk
cards: Atoms and nuclei emit and absorb

Changes in atoms and their nuclei can generate or absorb electromagnetic radiation over a wide range of frequencies. Gamma rays originate from nuclear changes; electron-level transitions are different. Transfer of energy does not require visible light.
Different waves, different hazards

Ultraviolet can cause premature skin ageing and increase skin-cancer risk. X-rays and gamma rays are ionising and can cause gene mutations and cancer. Risk depends on type and dose; a useful exposure can still carry risk. Draw conclusions from supplied data, not just the band’s name.
Compare dose consistently

A supplied dose may be in Sv or mSv;1000 mSv=1 Sv. The unit is not required recall, but comparisons need matching units. Evaluate consequences, exposure conditions, benefits and uncertainties. A detector count or an image brightness is not automatically a dose measurement.
Read a dose comparison

Choose a supplied dose in mSv and a number of equal exposures. Predict their total in mSv. This arithmetic is an invented same-condition comparison, not a personal medical-risk estimate or an assumption that biological responses always combine linearly.

extra.title: Higher: radio circuits oscillate
extra.text: Oscillations in an electrical circuit can produce radio waves. An incoming radio wave absorbed by a suitable circuit can induce an alternating current at the same frequency. Emission and reception transfer energy through oscillating electrical and electromagnetic systems; the detector does not have to be at the transmitter.

title: Using the electromagnetic spectrum
cards: Communication and heating

Radio waves carry radio/TV signals. Microwaves are used for satellite communication and cooking; infrared is used in electrical heaters, cooking and thermal cameras. Visible light is used for fibre-optic communication. The named band is linked to a useful interaction, not a unique speed in vacuum.
Light, imaging and treatment

Ultraviolet is used in energy-efficient lamps (with materials that emit visible light) and sun tanning, which carries skin risk. X-rays and gamma rays have medical imaging and treatment uses. Choose a wave according to what it must penetrate, transmit, detect or deposit energy in.
Compare alternatives

An infrared camera detects emitted infrared rather than seeing visible colour. A fibre carries a modulated light signal; it is not a sound pipe. Cooking uses energy absorbed by the food. Real communication systems also depend on atmosphere, bandwidth, detectors and engineering constraints.
Match a requirement

Choose a thermal-image or internal-transmission imaging requirement, then infrared or X-ray. Predict the stated match. This constrained selection illustrates a physical reason, not a universal product choice or clinical recommendation.

extra.text: Microwaves can pass through Earth’s atmosphere for satellite links; radio waves can carry broadcast signals; infrared is readily absorbed to warm surfaces and emitted by warm objects for thermal imaging. title: Lenses, ray diagrams and magnification
cards: Convex and concave lenses

A lens refracts light. A convex/converging lens brings incident parallel rays toward a principal focus; focal length is distance from lens centre to focus. A concave/diverging lens spreads parallel rays as if they came from a focus on the incoming side.
Construct the image

Use a ray parallel to the principal axis then through the far focus for a convex lens; a ray through the lens centre continues straight in the thin-lens model. Their crossing gives a real inverted image. With the object inside a convex focal length, extend emerging rays backward to find an upright virtual image. A concave lens forms a virtual image.
Real, virtual and magnified

A real image can be projected onto a screen; a virtual image is found by backward extensions and cannot be projected at that apparent location. Magnification=image height/object height, using the same length units; it has no unit. A converging lens can give real or virtual images depending on object position.
Compare image sizes

Choose object and supplied image heights, predict magnification and reveal a ray schematic. The actual image heights are supplied measurements, not a thin-lens-equation solution from the fixed drawing. Independent ray construction still needs your own correctly scaled diagram.

title: Visible colour, surfaces and filters
cards: Visible colours are wavelength bands

Each visible colour covers a narrow wavelength/frequency band. White light contains a mixture of visible wavelengths. A smooth surface reflects a beam in one direction (specular reflection); a rough surface scatters reflected rays (diffuse reflection).
Reflection gives an opaque object its colour

An opaque object appears the colour of wavelengths it reflects strongly under the available illumination. A red object reflects red and absorbs much other visible light; under only blue light it may look dark. White reflects visible wavelengths broadly; black absorbs them broadly.
Filters transmit selectively

A colour filter transmits selected wavelengths and absorbs others. A red filter transmits red; it cannot add red to a purely blue incoming beam. Transparent materials transmit a clear image; translucent materials transmit light but scatter it. Real filters have broad, imperfect transmission bands.
Predict a filter result

Choose an ideal red/blue incoming beam and red/blue filter. Predict transmitted colour or no beam. Colour labels accompany every outcome. This ideal single-band model omits partial transmission, perception and real spectral curves.

title: Black bodies and thermal emission
cards: Every object emits radiation

All objects emit and absorb infrared radiation regardless of temperature. A hotter object emits more energy per second. Temperature changes both emission intensity and the wavelength distribution: the peak shifts toward shorter wavelengths as temperature increases.
An ideal absorber and emitter

A perfect black body absorbs all radiation incident on it, with no reflection or transmission. A good absorber is also a good emitter, so a perfect black body is the best possible emitter at a given temperature. It is an ideal model, not simply any object painted black.
Read a spectrum

An emission spectrum plots intensity against wavelength. Hotter black-body curves are higher and peak at shorter wavelengths. A thermal camera’s false colours are chosen display colours; they do not mean a room-temperature object emits visible blue/red as drawn.
Compare ideal spectra

Choose a lower/higher supplied temperature and a low/high emitted-power comparison. Predict which spectrum peaks at shorter wavelength. The curves are qualitative illustrations, not Planck-law calculations or calibrated temperatures.

extra.title: Higher: balance incoming and outgoing radiation
extra.text: Constant temperature requires absorbed radiation power to equal emitted radiation power. If absorption exceeds emission, temperature rises; if emission exceeds absorption, it falls. Earth’s temperature depends on absorption, emission and reflection into space, including surface and atmospheric interactions. Compare energy-flow arrows and supplied values; a one-box model omits circulation, feedbacks and wavelength-dependent atmosphere.

title: Investigating infrared surfaces
cards: Compare the nature of surfaces

Required practical10 (separate) or21 (Trilogy) investigates how infrared absorbed or radiated depends on the surface. Compare matt black and shiny surfaces while controlling temperatures, area, distance, angle and detector settings. A Leslie cube with different faces can provide a common internal temperature for emission comparisons.
Measure emitted radiation

Keep detector position/distance and face area comparable; allow a stable temperature and record repeated readings. Matt dark surfaces are generally better emitters than shiny reflective surfaces at equal temperature. Detector readings are evidence under the apparatus conditions, not a universal colour-only law.
Investigate absorption fairly

Use identical containers/sensors and equal incident radiation/initial temperature. Compare temperature rise over the same time with other heat transfers controlled as far as possible. Avoid touching hot apparatus; follow school procedures. Conduction, convection and cooling can affect results.
Predict an illustrative reading

Choose matt/shiny surface and one of two common source temperatures. Predict which supplied relative detector reading applies. Values are original toy data, not emissivities or a complete cooling model. Physical apparatus use and uncertainty evaluation remain school evidence.
